reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: A histological diagnosis describing a neoplastic proliferation of epithelial cells within pre-existing prostatic ducts and acini while the basal cell layer remains intact
Graded as low-grade or high-grade, but only high-grade PIN (HGPIN) is regarded as a meaningful precursor of prostatic adenocarcinoma
It is an incidental biopsy finding that produces no specific symptoms and does not itself raise PSA
Multifocal or extensive HGPIN on biopsy carries a higher chance of finding cancer on subsequent sampling than a single focus
Isolated single-focus HGPIN no longer mandates immediate repeat biopsy under most current guidance, whereas multifocal HGPIN may prompt repeat or extended sampling
It is distinguished from atypical small acinar proliferation (ASAP), which carries a substantially higher likelihood of accompanying cancer and usually prompts early rebiopsy
Management is surveillance rather than treatment, since PIN is not itself invasive cancer
reference.pathophysiology: PIN represents dysplastic change within the luminal secretory epithelium of prostatic ducts and acini. The cells display nuclear enlargement and prominent nucleoli that resemble carcinoma, yet a basal cell layer is retained, separating the lesion from invasive disease. It is thought to arise through the accumulation of genetic and epigenetic changes and shares molecular alterations with adenocarcinoma, supporting a precursor role, particularly in the peripheral zone where most cancers originate.
additionalInvestigations: Histopathological review, ideally by a specialist uropathologist, to confirm grade and focality
Immunohistochemistry for basal cell markers (high-molecular-weight cytokeratin, p63) and AMACR to separate PIN from invasive carcinoma
PSA monitoring as part of overall prostate cancer risk assessment
Multiparametric MRI to identify suspicious areas for targeted rebiopsy
Repeat or targeted biopsy when HGPIN is multifocal or ASAP coexists
Documentation of the number of cores involved and the extent of involvement
redFlags: Coexisting atypical small acinar proliferation, which raises the probability of undetected cancer
A rising PSA or an MRI lesion suggesting occult carcinoma
A strong family history or other risk factors amplifying concern for cancer
reference.prognosis: PIN is not itself malignant and does not shorten life; the significance of high-grade PIN lies in an increased likelihood of concurrent or subsequent prostate cancer, which appropriate surveillance aims to detect.
pitfalls: Treating PIN as though it were cancer and offering radical therapy
Ignoring multifocal HGPIN or coexisting ASAP that warrants rebiopsy
Confusing clinically inconsequential low-grade PIN with high-grade PIN
Assuming PIN explains a raised PSA and thereby missing an underlying cancer
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Recognise that PIN is not itself malignant and requires no direct treatment, only appropriate follow-up for the associated cancer risk
Confirm the grade and focality on specialist uropathology review, using basal-cell markers and AMACR to exclude invasive carcinoma
Do not routinely rebiopsy isolated single-focus high-grade PIN; instead continue PSA monitoring and clinical follow-up
Arrange repeat, extended or targeted biopsy for multifocal or extensive high-grade PIN, or when atypical small acinar proliferation coexists
Use multiparametric MRI to identify suspicious areas for targeted rebiopsy
Continue PSA surveillance within overall prostate cancer risk assessment and refer to urology for ongoing monitoring
